title: The saloks to Mardana
hook: a few saloks are headed with Mardana's name, generally read as Nanak's words to him (Bihagra ki Var, ang 553)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Var: a quarrel, a return, and a song kept in the Granth. Your line was forgiven, and sung. Did you let someone back into the conversation? Day seven hundred ninety-three.

Mardana. In the Sikh stories he is close by: Guru Nanak's companion on the road, a Muslim musician with a rebab, playing while Nanak sang. Yesterday's minstrels came later. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to Bihagra ki Var, Ang 553. Among the saloks there, a few carry Mardana's name in the heading. They are generally read as Nanak's words to him, friend to friend. And they are not gentle words.
screen: `MARDANA AND HIS REBAB.` → `HIS NAME IN THE HEADING.` → `NANAK'S WORDS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: The saloks begin with a picture a friend might use to tease you awake. In paraphrase: this dark age is the wine jar, desire is the wine, and the mind is the one drinking it. Anger is the cup, filled with attachment, and ego is the one pouring. Drink in that company, and you're ruined. Strong words. But look where they go next, because Nanak doesn't just take the cup away. He offers a different brew. In paraphrase again: make good deeds the vat, truth the sweetener, and truth itself the finest wine. Make goodness the bread and good conduct the butter. That's the drink, he says, that wipes away wrongdoing. So the saloks don't scold the thirst. They redirect it. Whatever pulls at you, desire, the need to be filled, take that same longing and point it at truth. Now the heading. Readers differ on what the name Mardana is doing there: whether the words are spoken to him, or carry his name for another reason. The tradition generally hears them as words to a friend. And that changes how they sound. These aren't lines shouted at a crowd. They're the kind of thing you say to someone you've walked with for years, who can take hard words because they know you love them. Friends do that. They name the cup in your hand. Then they hand you a better one.
screen: `THE AGE IS THE JAR, DESIRE THE WINE.` · `A DIFFERENT BREW: DEEDS, TRUTH, GOODNESS.` · `NOT SCOLDING THE THIRST: REDIRECTING IT.` · `HARD WORDS, BETWEEN FRIENDS.` · then, large: `WORDS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: For the practice, talk kindly with a friend. In the sit, bring to mind a friend who has walked with you a long way. Think of a moment they told you something true that you didn't want to hear, or a moment you wish you had. Notice how kindness and honesty can sit in the same sentence. Then think of one kind thing you could say to that friend today, true and warm. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mardana. Guru Nanak's companion and rebab player, generally heard as the friend addressed in these saloks: trade the old cup for the wine of truth.
Your line: words to a friend. Today, send one friend a message that is both kind and true. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana as Guru Nanak's companion and rebab player, and the saloks headed with his name in Bihagra ki Var are read and sung as part of that Var.

fork.reveal: the saloks name desire as the wine and ego as the one pouring, then offer a new brew: good deeds, truth, goodness.

notes: Paraphrase of the saloks (kal kalvaalee kaam mad manooaa peevanhaar; krodh katoree mohi bharee daataa haumai ...; karnee laahan sat gur sach saraa kar saar; gun mande kar seel ghio ...): confirm images and which salok each belongs to.
'Scholars discuss what the name Mardana is doing there' and 'generally read as Nanak's words to him' (from the index): confirm; some read the heading as attributing the salok to Mardana.
Mardana as a Muslim rebab player and Guru Nanak's companion: from tradition (janamsakhis); stated in the hook as what the stories say.
'Yesterday's minstrels came later, in the same tradition of rebab players': confirm the connection between Mardana and later rababis such as Satta and Balvand is fair.
